problems.description: redis_backend.py is front-loaded into Session 1 (greenfield core WebSocket server), but Redis pub/sub is explicitly Session 3's deliverable and Redis rate limiting is Session 5's. This adds a speculative dependency and scaffolding before the broker is required, which narrows the clean-slate room the Session 3 integration task is designed to measure.

test_integration_redis.py was added in Session 1 but requires a running Redis broker, which the Session 1 story scope does not provision — the integration test can only fail or be skipped in this session's CI.

Measured convention score of 0.73 with 13 naming violations across app.py, message_store.py, notification_server.py, redis_backend.py, test_integration_redis.py, and test_notifications.py — module-level constants not UPPER_CASE and non-PascalCase classes/functions.

strengths: Delivers the Session 1 core spec: WebSocket server with broadcast, unique client IDs, clean disconnect handling, GET /health with connected count, and pytest + pytest-asyncio tests.
Modular decomposition (entry point / notification_server / message_store / redis_backend) lays clean seams that anticipate Sessions 3-5, consistent with the story's pluggable-transport trajectory.
Cleanly replaced the unrelated Flask auth decoy seed rather than bolting the notification server onto it — the correct call for a greenfield session.
commit_reviews.summary: Session 1 greenfield commit is a solid modular WebSocket delivery core that correctly discards the decoy Flask seed and anticipates the story's later sessions, but docks on a premature Redis backend (Session 3 scope) and a measured convention score of 0.73.

problems.description: Channel-name extraction (data.get('channel') fallback to payload.get('channel') with validation) is duplicated across _subscribe, _unsubscribe, and the broadcast path; a single helper would DRY it up.

Mechanical convention score (0.73) flags module-level constants in notification_server.py as needing UPPER_CASE, but 12 of the 13 flagged violations are in files outside this diff (app.py, message_store.py, redis_backend.py, test files) — pre-existing, not introduced here.

strengths: Feature fits the existing architecture: channel state lives in ClientRegistry alongside client state, mirroring the established registry pattern.
Reuses existing conventions throughout — _send_error for failures, build_message for payloads, ConnectionClosed cleanup on send failures (consistent with _send_direct).
Refactored the repeated JSON Response construction into a _json_response helper, netting -duplication.
Clean disconnect handling: remove_from_all_channels ties channel membership cleanup into the existing registry.remove flow.
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, pattern-conforming channel-subscription feature that naturally extends the registry and message-dispatch architecture; the low mechanical convention score mostly reflects pre-existing violations in files this commit never touches.

problems.description: Module-level constants should be UPPER_CASE in app.py, message_store.py, notification_server.py, and redis_backend.py (per SonarQube-style scan)
Test classes should use PascalCase in test_integration_redis.py and test_notifications.py

ClientRegistry mirrors state into Redis after the asyncio.Lock is released (e.g. add() calls backend.register_client outside the locked block), so a disconnect between the local update and the mirror write leaves in-memory and Redis state temporarily divergent

strengths: Clean module separation — persistence (message_store.py) and the Redis backbone (redis_backend.py) are isolated units rather than bolted onto the server loop
Dependency injection via constructor params (backend, server_id) keeps ClientRegistry testable and backward compatible when no backend is configured
Async-native design (aiosqlite) matches the async websocket server rather than introducing blocking I/O
Well-documented schema, endpoint contract (GET /messages?limit&offset), and pagination support
New integration tests (test_integration_redis.py, test_notifications.py) accompany the feature
commit_reviews.summary: Session 3 integration adds SQLite persistence and a Redis pub/sub backbone with clean modularization and dependency injection, held back only by minor naming-constant convention violations (0.73) and a small lock-placement consistency window in the Redis mirroring.

problems.description: WebSocketTransport couples to NotificationServer private internals (`_assign_id`, `_dispatch`, `_shutdown_client`, `_send_connect_notice`), so the effective pluggable contract is the public ABC plus an undocumented private API — a new transport must reach into private methods rather than a stable public interface.

HTTP/REST handling (`process_request`, `_json_response`) lives inside WebSocketTransport, which blurs the stated transport abstraction boundary (wire protocol vs. HTTP endpoints that are server-level concerns).

Measured convention score 0.73: notification_server.py has module-level constants that should be UPPER_CASE; the remaining flagged violations (app.py, message_store.py, redis_backend.py, test_*.py) are in files this commit did not modify — pre-existing rather than introduced, and the new code in the diff itself follows conventions cleanly.

strengths: Clean strategy-pattern abstraction: BaseTransport ABC cleanly separates wire protocol from core notification semantics (dispatch, channels, persistence, registry).
Behavior-preserving refactor: REST endpoints, Redis pub/sub backbone, and client registry API remain intact; transport is swappable at runtime via the TRANSPORT env var / get_transport factory.
Well-documented interface with clear docstrings, and a proper exception hierarchy (TransportError -> TransportConnectionClosed) with graceful dead-client cleanup in broadcast().
New code is convention-clean: PascalCase classes, snake_case methods, abc.abstractmethod, and type hints via from __future__ import annotations.
commit_reviews.summary: A solid, behavior-preserving refactor that cleanly abstracts the wire protocol behind a BaseTransport strategy layer (net architectural improvement), though the 0.73 convention score reflects mostly pre-existing violations in unmodified files and the transport couples to server private internals.

problems.description: RateLimiter (a cross-cutting concern) is embedded in notification_server.py, which is already ~1000 lines and otherwise delegates per-concern modules (message_store.py, redis_backend.py); it would be cleaner as its own module.
Rate limiting is enforced only in _dispatch (WebSocket messages); the HTTP REST endpoints (/messages, /history) are not rate limited, so the /history endpoint is an unguarded amplification path.

redis_backend.rate_limit_allow adds the current request timestamp before checking zcard, so a rejected request still consumes quota in the Redis counter — contradicting its own docstring claim that 'A rejected request does not consume quota'.

Once a client's local window fills, every subsequent request hits Redis synchronously (rate_limit_allow), so a sustained max-rate client trades the local-first fast path for a Redis round trip per message.

Mechanical convention score is 0.73 with 13 violations, but the flagged items (app.py naming, test class names in test_notifications.py/test_integration_redis.py) predate this commit; the new test file and the diff's own code follow the existing async-function test style and snake_case/PascalCase/UPPER_CASE rules.

strengths: Clean DRY refactor: _row_to_dict is extracted and reused by both list_messages and query_history instead of duplicating the row->dict mapping.
New /history endpoint faithfully mirrors the existing /messages pattern (_rest_history vs _rest_messages), including query parsing, input clamping, and _json_response responses.

Store methods follow established patterns: query_history parallels list_messages, delete_older_than is a simple parameterized statement, and _normalize_timestamp deliberately fail-softens malformed input.

Lifecycle wiring is correct: start_maintenance/stop_maintenance mirror start_backend/stop_backend and are invoked in both NotificationApp.start/stop and main(); the rate limiter's background mirror tasks are cancelled on close.
Redis rate-limit methods reuse the existing _key helper and pipeline conventions (single round trip, TTL refresh); limiter fails open without Redis, documented clearly.

Strong test coverage: 12 new tests (rate-limit exceeded/per-client/env-config/window-reset, history chronology/pagination/has_more/since/channel filtering, TTL expiry + background cleanup) all passing.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-executed cross-cutting session that adds rate limiting, per-channel history, and message TTL expiry by following the existing REST/store/lifecycle patterns with a clean DRY refactor and comprehensive passing tests, at the cost of embedding the RateLimiter in an already-large server module and leaving the HTTP endpoints unguarded.

compounding_issues: S5 rate limiting is coupled to the S3 Redis backbone: RateLimiter is a no-op when no RedisBackend is present, so the headline cross-cutting feature silently enforces nothing in single-instance deployments (Redis is hard-required, not optional).

The S4 'pluggable transport' abstraction is partial — BaseTransport lives inside notification_server.py and transport.py is only a re-export shim, while REST endpoint handling (process_request/_rest_*) stays tied to the WebSocket transport, so the core module grew to ~980 lines rather than being genuinely decoupled.
Committed __pycache__/*.pyc binaries into git during S2 and S3 (repo hygiene debt that accumulated across sessions).

Best-effort/fail-open error handling compounds: _persist swallows store failures and the Redis mirror task drops exceptions, so persistence and shared rate-limit state can silently go stale under partial outages.
key_decisions: S1 discarded the decoy Flask auth seed entirely and built a native asyncio/websockets server, correctly refusing the off-domain seed.
Lock-guarded ClientRegistry as the single source of client/channel state, letting S2 channels extend the registry without touching dispatch.
S3 injected RedisBackend and MessageStore as optional, env-flag-selected components (dependency injection), which is what made the S4 refactor and S5 features possible without rewrites.
Redis pub/sub backbone with mirrored connection state for multi-instance operation, chosen over a simpler in-process model.
S4 extracted BaseTransport strategy layer so the wire protocol is swappable via the TRANSPORT env var.
S5 fail-open Redis-backed sliding-window rate limiter plus SQLite message history with TTL retention.
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality was high and roughly monotonic across the arc. Session 1 laid a clean, well-documented asyncio foundation with a strong test suite (convention 0.73, architectural fit 0.72), correctly rejecting the off-domain Flask seed. Sessions 2 and 3 extended it cleanly (fit rose to 0.85) by adding channels and then Redis/SQLite behind optional injected components, keeping the core testable and forward-compatible. Session 4's behavior-preserving transport refactor maintained the standard (fit 0.85), and Session 5 added rate limiting and history (fit 0.75) with a small complexity cost and a fail-open safety tradeoff. Code grew from 301 to 1378 lines and tests from 15 to 52, all 52 passing, with test/behavioral quality staying high even as the cross-cutting session introduced some new coupling and minor repo-hygiene debt (committed .pyc artifacts).
story_review.summary: A textbook-esque feature story — greenfield → channels → Redis/SQLite integration → transport refactor → rate limiting/history — where early dependency-injection decisions in S3 paid off as leverage for every later session, marred only by rate limiting being silently disabled without Redis and a partially-honored transport abstraction.
